data.title: The Memo: Weak jobs report clouds economy as Trump barrels toward midterms
data.description:
New clouds darkened the economic landscape on Friday, as the latest employment report showed the nation shedding 23,000 jobs in July.

The number came as an unpleasant surprise to most economists. The consensus prediction from experts canvassed by Dow Jones had been that more than 80,000 jobs would be created.

Democrats pounced on the number to reinforce their case that President Trump is mismanaging the economy.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, wrote on social media platform X: “The economic failures of the Trump administration keep piling up. There’s no way to spin these dismal results, because Americans know they’re paying the price every day.”

Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif,), the former Speaker, chimed in that, “Today’s disastrous report is the latest proof that the Trump economy has failed the American people.”

And Abdul El-Sayed, who this week won the Democratic nomination to battle former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in a U.S. Senate race in Michigan, wrote: “Trump dump…or slump. Either way, it’s bad. Mike Rogers wants to rubber stamp this. I want to stand up to it.”

Democrats believed even before the latest report that the economy would be a strong issue for them in November’s midterm elections.

Trump was elected, at least in part, to ease inflation that had lingered since hitting its highest point in decades in the middle of the Biden presidency.

Progress has been slow and, in recent months, has gone in the wrong direction, however. That’s largely because of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran and the consequent climb in the price of oil.

Inflation peaked under Biden at an annualized rate of 9.1 percent in June 2022. But it had fallen to 2.7 percent by November 2024, the month in which Trump defeated then-Vice President Harris.

The inflation figure now has been above 3 percent every month since the war on Iran began on Feb. 28. It hit 4.2 percent in May and stood at 3.5 percent for June. New figures covering July will be released next Wednesday.

The public is feeling the effects both of persistent inflation and a broader sense of economic malaise.

According to the polling averages maintained by RealClearPolitics, Trump’s single worst issue is inflation, with more than two-thirds of the public disapproving of his performance. 

On the economy in general, Trump doesn’t fare much better: Roughly 61 percent of people disapprove of his performance while about 37 percent approve.

But there are some caveats, for sure. 

Trump often focuses on the performance of the stock market as an indicator of the economy’s health. The president frequently notes how gains on Wall Street are good news for Americans with 401(k) retirement savings plans as well as for people who hold stocks directly.

The S&P 500, the most broad-based of the three major stock market indices, rose again on Friday, closing at 7,757. That’s a gain of almost 30 percent since Trump was inaugurated in January 2025.

The fact that the market rose on Friday, after a poor jobs report, is not as strange as it might seem.

Broadly speaking, Wall Street’s primary concern is interest rates. 

The markets fear that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates soon to try to fight inflation. But a bad jobs report makes that slightly less likely, since the central bank might think the economy is slowing of its own accord and needs no further pumping of the brakes.

Mark Zandi, chief economist with Moody’s Analytics, noted that there are other indicators, such as decelerating wage growth and comparatively “tame” rises in housing costs, that also weigh against a rate increase.

“There are a lot of gravitational forces to bring inflation back in,” Zandi told this column. “Given the weak economy, I would be holding rates steady. What will [the Fed] do? I think this jobs report strengths the hand of people who want to keep rates unchanged.”

Trump and his allies take issue with the claim that the economy is weak, however.

Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House’s National Economic Council, told reporters on Friday, “The economy continues to be strong. We see durable goods orders, capital spending, through the roof. People aren’t being laid off.”

Hassett also played down the jobs report as “very noisy data… It’s a survey that is, like, one thing to look at but there are a lot of other things to look at too.”

Some Trump allies also note that even as the nation lost jobs, the unemployment rate ticked down, from 4.2 percent in June to 4.1 percent in July.  

But, again, that is shaky grounds for optimism.

The unemployment rate decrease is a byproduct of people leaving the labor market. 

Economists debate whether this is the consequence of people giving up on finding jobs or being able to retire early, or whether it is caused by immigrants — authorized as well as unauthorized — leaving the U.S.

Whatever the reason, a smaller labor force typically results in less robust economic growth.

There is, of course, the possibility that public sentiment about the economy will improve — perhaps if the conflict in Iran is definitively ended and prices come down.

But time is running short for Trump and the GOP with the midterms just three months away. 

And Friday’s jobs report certainly didn’t help.

“There’s absolutely no reason to see any sunshine in this,” said Zandi. “It’s just shades of gray and black.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: Senate embarks on recess after funding government and confirming Blanche, punting other priorities
data.description:
The Senate adjourned for a five-week recess early Saturday morning after passing a bill to fund the federal government until Dec. 11 and confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general.

Senate Republicans also agreed to set aside — for the moment — President Trump’s demand to approve another budget resolution to pave the way for tens of billions of dollars in new military spending and to pass the SAVE America Act.

Senators will return to their home states or take congressional delegation trips abroad for the next several weeks and are not due to return to Washington until Sept. 14.

Passage of the continuing resolution to fund the government past the election takes a lot of pressure off senators in both parties ahead of the September work period as both Democrats and Republicans were eager to avoid stumbling into another government shutdown before the midterm election.

The stopgap funding measure passed 90 to 6, with Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) voting present because the legislation includes a death benefit for her brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) heir.

The funding bill was held up by an intense fight within the Senate GOP conference over a provision added at the behest of the White House to delay the implementation of a ban on  intoxicating hemp-derived products that Congress enacted in November.

Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) insisted on voting on an amendment to strip the hemp-related language out of the bill but the Senate voted 61-32 to table it.

The Senate later voted largely along party lines to narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general.

Two Republicans, Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), voted against Blanche, citing their concerns about whether he would maintain the Justice Department’s political independence.

Collins said that Blanche’s actions as deputy attorney general had “further eroded the department’s independence” and Murkowski said the “politicization” and “weaponization” of the Justice Department has “accelerated” under Blanche’s leadership.

Blanche’s nomination was saved from derailment, however, when Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who had been undecided for weeks, announced on Friday morning that he would vote yes.

“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche,” Cassidy he said on the Senate floor, adding with a tone of resignation: “I will be criticized for this vote. What’s new?”

The Senate voted 50-49 to confirm Blanche, with Collins, Murkowski and all Democrats voting against him.

A key development came late Friday evening when Senate conservatives relented on their demands that the Senate stay in session until Republicans pass a budget resolution to set up a third budget reconciliation bill to fund the Pentagon and the SAVE America Act, Trump’s No. 1 legislative priority.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) agreed to postpone action on the budget resolution until after the August recess after it became clear that it probably would not get 50 votes to advance on the Senate floor.

Johnson and conservative Sens. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) spoke to Trump Friday evening to get his approval for a plan to allow the Senate to adjourn without action on either measure.

Johnson, Lee and Scott agreed to postpone action on the budget resolution and further debate of the SAVE America Act, which would require people to prove citizenship when registering to vote and show photo identification to vote, after holding a two-hour meeting with GOP colleagues just off the Senate floor.

“There was a concern whether or not it could actually pass, the budget resolution, tonight,” Johnson acknowledged.

Conservatives instead got Thune and the rest of their colleagues to agree to set up a vote on a bill sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) to require voters to show photo identification in federal elections.

That measure later failed to advance on the floor. It received 52 votes but fell eight short of the 60 needed to move forward.

Lee indicated that he would not force Republican colleagues to hold a roll-call vote on a politically sensitive adjournment resolution in order to start the recess because he was satisfied with the agreement to vote on the Husted proposal.

“We’re not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it right now,” he said of the SAVE America Act.

Thune was able to schedule a series of rapid, overnight votes that allowed the Senate to begin the recess after reaching a deal with Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to postpone action on a bill crafted by the Senate Commerce Committee to establish rules and standards for the compensation and recruitment of college athletes until September.

A disagreement over whether to hold votes to proceed to the college sports bill and then approve it with a 60-vote threshold had delayed a broader agreement on speeding up the procedural timeline for the continuing resolution and Blanche had stalled Senate action for much of Thursday and Friday.

data.title: Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general after bruising fight
data.description:
The Senate early Saturday morning confirmed Todd Blanche as the next attorney general, with the nominee narrowly securing sufficient GOP backing after making a number of promises about how he would handle his tenure as the country’s top law enforcement officer.

The vote was 50-49.

Though confirmed along a party-line vote when he was nominated as deputy attorney general in March of last year, Blanche faltered in gaining GOP support to lead the Justice Department after a series of actions that earned pushback from skeptical Republicans.

Chief among them was Blanche’s decision to sign off on a $1.776 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund expected to funnel money to Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants. The fund, which Blanche formally rescinded earlier this week, was created in the wake of an agreement to settle a $10 billion suit from President Trump brought against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

Blanche was able to clinch confirmation with the reluctant backing of Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who took to the Senate floor Friday morning to announce and explain his much-anticipated decision.

“The choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche; it is between Mr. Blanch and another acting attorney general, who may not run the department effectively under President Trump, and who indeed may not be as good as Mr. Blanche,” he said.

But Blanche failed to get the support of Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who both cited concerns about the ability of President Trump’s former personal attorney to exert independence as head of the Justice Department. Both also pointed out that the fund could easily be revived in court.

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” Murkowski wrote Friday in announcing her decision not to support him.

She blasted Blanche for a related memo that gave Trump, his adult children, and their businesses sweeping immunity for their past conduct, including outstanding audits that could yield significant tax bills.

“I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” she wrote.

Collins earlier this week said that while she believed “Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political.”

“Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation,” she said, noting his pledge to restrict abortion medication and another order giving Trump and his adult children immunity from being investigated for their past actions, including failure to pay taxes.

Cassidy also blasted the arrangement despite his support for Blanche.

“Mr. Blanche showed poor judgment in approving the anti-weaponization slush fund and exempting the president from IRS audits. No American should be unfairly targeted by the law, but no American should be above the law,” he said.

Cassidy’s eleventh-hour backing of Blanche avoided what could have been a significant delay in the confirmation. Without his vote, the chamber may have been forced to wait until the return of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), whose intentions on the attorney are unclear.

Blanche faced unusually steep resistance from Republicans on this path to securing the promotion.

A vote to advance him out of the Senate Judiciary Committee had to be postponed when GOP Sens. Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) vowed to oppose him if he did not memorialize in writing his pledge that the fund is “not moving forward. Period.” 

Blanche did so after days of haggling, but it does not prohibit Trump from going to court to seek to revive the matter. Nor does it kill the sweeping immunity order that gives Trump and his family broad immunity from any government review of their past conduct, including tax audits.

The Justice Department has not yet asserted the rescission of the fund in the multitude of related court cases it faces, and Trump has appealed a ruling in his IRS case that found his lawsuit was collusive in nature.

Blanche also faced questions from lawmakers over DOJ’s efforts to investigate six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military service members have the right to refuse any illegal orders.

Cassidy has said that issue was a top concern for him, though in his floor speech he suggested Blanche had agreed to abandon the case.

“I will note that I’ve learned that some of the cases that have been publicly reported to be under investigation by the Department of Justice have been dismissed or are no longer being pursued. I am realistic that President Trump can be unrelenting on this, but this will be true no matter who the Attorney General is, and this is the rationale for having a Senate confirmed Attorney General with more leverage to push back,” Cassidy said.

Democrats, similarly to Murkowski and Collins, also tore into Blanche over his handling of a number of other issues, from his handling of the Epstein files to numerous cases brought against Trump foes.

Several Democrats also accused Blanche of lying under oath, including to Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), who noted that the attorney told her in a hearing he had rescinded the order, yet the rescission he publicly released showed it was signed Sunday.

“He testified that he had rescinded it. In questions for the record, I asked him, ‘Give me the date of when you rescinded this order and this fund.’ He did not answer the question with a date. He refused to end this fund in writing until he was forced into it in order to secure needed votes from my Republican colleagues,” she said Tuesday.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) pointed to Blanche’s previous role as Trump’s personal attorney.

“We should not confirm an attorney general who views his job as enriching the president of the United States….We should not confirm an attorney general who believes that the president has a right and a duty to go after his political enemies,” Schiff said earlier this week as the Senate Judiciary Committee weighed the nomination.

“The problem with confirming Todd Blanch is that he has never been able to shed his role as criminal defense lawyer for Donald Trump. He just can’t do it. He does not represent the American people now. He will never represent the American people. He will never do what’s best for the American people. He will only do what’s best for Donald Trump, and you cannot leave someone like that as the nation’s number one law enforcement official.”

Democrats also raised the widespread firings carried out by the Justice Department, including of those who worked on Jan. 6 cases, as well as the demotions a number of other key attorneys.

Justice Connection, a DOJ alumni group, previously sent a letter signed by 1,200 former employees opposed to Blanche, a remarkable number in urging the Senate to reject his nomination.

“Unlike most nominees who come before the Senate, Todd Blanche has spent four months as DOJ’s top dog and a year as second-in-charge. He’s used that time to shred DOJ’s institutional norms, destroy important offices, revictimize sex crime survivors, eviscerate accountability for January 6, attack the career workforce. By serving as the president’s sword and shield, he’s unraveled the rule of law – leaving our rights, economic interests, safety, and democracy on shaky ground,” Stacey Young, a former DOJ official and the group’s executive director, said in a statement.

“Nearly 20,000 career employees have left the department, many of whom were fired or forced out for doing their jobs. This is a generational loss of institutional knowledge and expertise that will be impossible to replace. Today’s vote is an affront to the dedicated public servants still there, as they struggle to uphold the law under a leader who doesn’t.”

data.title: Senate tables hemp amendment at center of funding fight, allowing one-month delay of ban
data.description:
A federal ban on most hemp-derived THC products is set to be delayed for a month after a last-minute effort to keep the original timeline failed. 

The Senate voted 61-32 to table a bipartisan amendment from Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) and about a dozen other senators to strip the delay from a stopgap government funding bill.

Opponents of the delay had been holding up consideration of the funding bill until GOP leadership allowed a vote on the amendment.  

The provision at the heart of the controversy was inserted into the underlying legislation at the behest of the White House, which has made delaying or otherwise fixing the hemp ban a priority. 

Hemp industry groups and their allies are touting the provision as a significant win that will give them more time to convince lawmakers to regulate their products, rather than ban them. 

But the fight isn’t over, and Budd and the other supporters of his effort have indicated they will try again in the fall and winter. The funding bill lasts through Dec. 11, and White House officials have reportedly told senators they will not ask for another delay. 

Trump signed the ban into law last year as part of a broader spending bill to reopen the government after a record-long shutdown. It was set to take effect Nov. 12. 

The legislation redefined hemp to close what critics called the “hemp loophole” brought about by the 2018 Farm Bill, which removed hemp from the controlled substances list. The fix was championed by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) 

The hemp industry has been lobbying furiously against it ever since, arguing the law would collapse a multi-billion-dollar industry. 

Budd and other supporters say they are trying to protect children from illicit products that are intentionally marketed to children. The products are labeled as hemp, but contain extremely high levels of synthetic THC, the psychedelic compound in marijuana responsible for a high.    

On Friday, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services administrator Mehmet Oz urged senators to oppose the amendment because it could interfere with an agency pilot program allowing access to certain hemp-derived products.  

Budd said getting rid of unregulated products won’t do the damage Oz alleges. 

“Why do unregulated intoxicating edibles need to be available at gas stations for CMS to continue studying hemp-derived pain relief?” Budd wrote on social media.  

 “Why should we allow these products on shelves for one more day when someone could make a decision that will alter their future by buying them?”

data.title: Senate passes stopgap funding bill to prevent shutdown ahead of midterms
data.description:
The Senate voted early Saturday morning to fund the federal government until Dec. 11 with the aim of averting another government shutdown before the midterm election, sending the bill to the House before leaving for a five-week recess.

The continuing resolution (CR) passed 90-6 after Republicans spent days haggling over a provision inserted by the White House into the legislation that would have delayed a ban on hemp-derived THC products until December.

The legislation includes another provision demanded by Democrats and some Republicans on the Appropriations Committee, including Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), to temporarily halt a rule from the White House budget office that would give political appointees in the executive branch more authority over dispersing federal grants.

Democrats insisted that the short-term funding measure needed to include language to freeze the White House budget office’s rulemaking if it was to pass before September, according to senators familiar with the bipartisan negotiations.

Collins, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, also opposed the White House budget office rulemaking, calling it “deeply flawed.”

She asked Russ Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, in a letter last month to withdraw the rule.

The vote on the continuing resolution finally came early Saturday morning after Republicans spent hours battling among themselves over setting up a series of votes to fund the government, confirm Attorney General Todd Blanche, and require voters to show photo identification for federal elections.

The final agreement to speed up consideration of the stopgap government funding measure was delayed for much of Thursday and Friday because of a disagreement over how to handle a separate bill crafted by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) to set new rules for recruiting and compensating college athletes.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) announced the early-morning vote to fund the government after Cruz agreed to delay floor consideration of the Protect College Sports Act until September.

The measure now goes to the House, which is scheduled to return on Aug. 31, for a vote.

Federal funding is due to expire on Sept. 30 without action from Congress.

Some House Republicans may not be thrilled about the provisions that quash the White House budget office’s rulemaking to exert more executive-branch authority over congressionally funded grants.

House fiscal conservatives, in particular, may balk at an extension of federal funding without spending cuts to reduce the deficit.

But the passage of the Senate-approved measure is hardly in doubt after it passed with such an overwhelming margin in the upper chamber.

Usually, Congress passes short-term government funding measures shortly before funding is due to lapse. But with the midterm elections less than three months away, lawmakers in both parties didn’t want to risk until waiting until late September to fund the government.

Both Republican and Democratic senators were eager to avoid another protracted standoff after enduring a record-breaking 43-day government shutdown in October and November.

That grueling fight was followed by another fierce partisan battle over funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol that caused the Department of Homeland Security to shut down earlier this year.  

“I think it’s the most important thing for us to do,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.). “Because I don’t think we need to have the harbinger of a possible government shutdown. So, take it off the table. I think we all want to do that.”

Some Republicans had warned for months that Democrats would try to shut down the government right before the midterm election in order to accuse Republicans of not being up to the task of governing.

“I think my Democratic friends are going to shut down the government right before the midterms,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) warned in the spring.

Thune made passing a funding bill to keep the government open past the election one of his top priorities before the August recess.

He warned that he would use the budget reconciliation process to fund the entire federal government if Democrats blocked the continuing resolution under regular order. Budget reconciliation enables the minority party to circumvent a filibuster.

In the end, however, Democrats were as eager as Republicans to avoid another shutdown.

“For months, Democrats have been clear: we want to fund the government, avoid a shutdown, and pass strong, bipartisan appropriations bills that improve people’s lives,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said in a statement.

Quick passage of the funding measure was complicated by an animated fight among Republicans over language slipped into the bill at the White House’s request to delay the implementation of a ban on hemp-derived intoxicants such as delta-8, which are often sold at gas stations and not approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

Republican senators were caught off guard by the late addition of the provision delaying the ban and some of them vented their frustration with White House legislative staff over the issue at a tense lunch meeting on Tuesday.

Some Republicans, however, supported delaying the ban on hemp-related products to support the hemp industries in their state, including Sen. Rand Paul (R) of Kentucky and Sens. Steve Daines (R) and Tim Sheehy (R) of Montana.

The GOP critics of the proposal to delay the ban led by Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) attempted to strip it out of the bill but senators voted 61 to 32 to table Budd’s amendment to do so.

Budd warned on the Senate floor before the vote that Congress last year voted to ban the unregulated sale of intoxicating hemp products

“These products are made to look exactly like something a kid would want. Emergency Departments have seen a 461-percent increase in cases of pediatric cannabis poisoning. Most of those were children four years old or younger,” he said.

Sheehy, in a video uploaded to social media, argued hemp-derived products have “provided in many cases a natural and healthy way” for people suffering from pain, such as military veterans, to find relief.

“That’s been life-changing for a lot of people. A lot of them I know personally, which is why I’ve taken up this cause,” he said.

data.title: Thune, Trump, Senate conservatives reach deal to set aside budget, SAVE America Act impasse
data.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), President Trump and Senate conservatives reached a deal Friday night to set aside a vote on a budget resolution and defer action on much of the SAVE America Act until after the August recess, settling a fight that had divided Senate Republicans for weeks.

Conservative Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) emerged from Thune’s office in the Capitol after speaking with Trump and holding a two-hour conference meeting with GOP colleagues, and told reporters they had reached an agreement.

They said that there’s now consensus within the conference to postpone action on a Senate budget resolution that would serve as a blueprint for a reconciliation bill until after the August recess and to vote immediately on a key element of the SAVE America Act — the requirement that voters show photo identification in federal elections.

Johnson, Lee and Scott, who have called on Senate GOP colleagues to cancel the August recess to debate and attempt to pass the full SAVE America Act, acknowledged they didn’t have the votes to advance that bill anytime soon.

“We had about a two-hour conference meeting, trying to figure out what we need to do to come to an agreement to accomplish what the president wanted,” Johnson said, acknowledging that the proposed budget resolution may have failed on the Senate floor because of a lack of enough Republican support.

“There was a concern whether or not it could actually pass, the budget resolution, tonight,” he said, noting that some colleagues wanted substantially more funding for the Pentagon than the $73 billion proposed in a House-passed budget resolution. The budget resolution would serve as a blueprint for a party-line reconciliation bill Republicans aim to pass without needing Democratic support.

“There’s certainly concern in terms of the need for our military. When the finest among us are in harm’s way, is it really enough?” Johnson said. “The conclusion of the conference and then we had the discussion with the president, he agrees, don’t take the vote tonight. Just work diligently through August and September to do an actually better budget reconciliation bill.”

“We’re all satisfied with that. So, we’re not going to vote on budget resolution tonight and really work hard tonight,” he said.

The conservative leaders say they’re also “hopeful” on finding a way to vote soon on a continuing resolution to fund the government through Dec. 11 and to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general. Republicans had spent much of Friday searching for a deal to accelerate the timeframe for passing both priorities.

Lee indicated that he would not force Republican colleagues to vote on a politically sensitive adjournment resolution in order to embark on a five-week recess because he was satisfied with an emerging agreement to vote instead on a bill sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) to require voters to show photo identification in federal elections.

Lee said “of course” he’s disappointed that the SAVE America Act won’t pass anytime soon but acknowledged “we’re not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it right now.”

“But we are going to vote on a handful of things, including the Husted measure with photo ID, which is about half of what the SAVE America Act is,” Lee said. “That will give us some indication of where we stand.

“Voter ID is a major component of SAVE America,” he added.

Democrats defeated Husted’s proposal to require voters to show voter identification in a 53-47 vote when he offered it as an amendment on Senate floor in March. The vote came during a lengthy debate on the SAVE America Act, which Senate Democrats have repeatedly blocked.

Democrats voted against Husted’s amendment in March despite Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s (N.Y.) claim that Democrats support photo ID requirements for elections.

Schumer told reporters in a March 15 press call that Democrats included a voter ID provision in their Freedom to Vote Act, which they introduced in 2021 when they controlled the Senate.

“Democrats support voter ID. In fact, we included it and it is included in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago. So, we’re not opposed,” Schumer said.

Lee said conservatives want to put Democrats on the record on the issue once again.

“We’ve got many Democrats who’ve said, ‘I’m just fine with voter ID.’” Lee said. “We’re going to find out where they are on that.”

Johnson said Trump signed off on the plan to wrap up the Senate’s work before the August recess.

“We’re in total agreement. There’s no argument about it,” he said.

The Senate has already voted five times on the SAVE America Act or major elements of it but have failed to entice enough Democrats to overcome the 60-vote threshold for ending a filibuster.

Thune has repeatedly said that Senate Republicans don’t have the votes to abolish the filibuster to pass election reform legislation, as Trump has demanded.

data.title: TPS protections terminated for Myanmar, South Sudan migrants
data.description:
Two U.S. district judges rejected cases defending temporary protections for migrants from South Sudan and Myanmar, leaving some at risk for deportation.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued two alerts on its website confirming that, effective Aug. 7, Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation had been halted for both countries.

The notice came after U.S. District Judge Patti Saris of Boston rejected an attempt by an immigrant-advocacy organization to protect South Sudanese migrants currently living in the U.S. under TPS protections. A similar decision followed hours later by District Judge Matthew Kennelly of Chicago for migrants from Myanmar.

TPS was created under the Immigration Act of 1990 — providing temporary, lawful immigration status in the U.S. for certain foreign nationals who are already in the country and are from countries to where the government has deemed returning unsafe.

South Sudan received the TPS designation in 2011 due to the civil war while Myanmar was designated in 2021 based on “extraordinary and temporary conditions.”

DHS initially attempted to end TPS protections for both countries in November, but at the time, Saris and Kennelly rejected the proposals. A June Supreme Court decision laid the groundwork for the federal judges’ decisions, with justices then ruling to end TPS protections for migrants from Haiti and Syria.

The high court ruled in a 6-3 decision, along ideological lines, that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to TPS terminations — allowing federal authorities to continue.

The loss of TPS will impact around 4,200 South Sudanese and Myanmar migrants, Reuters reported.

Myanmar is still being led by an army that overthrew the government and detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi. In February, the United Nations warned that South Sudan was on a “dangerous precipice,” as violence continued to escalate in the country.

data.title: Spencer Pratt says he's working with Trump on 25 percent federal film tax credit
data.description:
Reality TV star and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt said in a recent post that he is working with President Trump on a 25 percent federal film tax.

In a Friday post on the social platform X, Pratt stated the move was to “bring back Hollywood.”

“I’m committed to saving Hollywood, and I’m very grateful for the President’s remarkable generosity and focus on this issue,” Pratt said. “He is very passionate about revitalizing the entertainment industry and we will not let Canada, or the UK or Budapest steal our lunch anymore.”

He attached two pictures of a lunch he had with Trump during the president’s visit to California. 

“Unlike many other cynical doomers out there, he refuses to write off California. We are only getting started,” Pratt concluded in his post.

Pratt received Trump’s endorsement while running for Los Angeles mayor but was eliminated in the primaries. Progressive City Council member Nithya Raman narrowly beat him out to compete in a runoff election against incumbent mayor Karen Bass. 

After the results were announced, Trump wrote on social media that it is “not possible for Spencer Pratt to have lost the L.A. runoffs after the big lead he had, 3rd World Nation. Rigged Elections!”

This followed claims from other Republicans that commented on California’s lengthy election process.

Polls reported Pratt was solidly in second place when the in-person polls closed on June 2, but then saw his eight-point lead over Raman evaporate as mail-in ballots were counted in the week following the election day.

“I’m not going to defend any of California’s election process. I think it’s crazy that it takes that long to count votes, I really do,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said about the race but chose to not echo Trump’s claim.

data.title: Trump maintains vandalism claims, calls on Pirro to 're-visit' Reflecting Pool
data.description:
President Trump is asking the Justice Department (DOJ) to reconsider its move to drop criminal charges against those accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, continuing to assert vandalism was to blame for its appearance.

Trump specifically urged U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro to “re-visit her hastily made decision” in a Friday Truth Social post.

Despite the president’s claims, Pirro’s office has said contractors who led renovation efforts on the national monument were responsible for the damage.

The president shared a screenshot of an X post made by freelance photographer Andrew Leyden, which Trump claimed showed proof of vandalism in the pool. Leyden captioned his original pictures claiming he had seen “cuts in the expansion joints on the side of the Reflecting Pool.”

“The material was cut right where the video tape showed, for 300 feet or more. People were on their knees with their hands in the water at the exact location of the ‘slashes,’” Trump wrote. “Additionally, there were witnesses to the VANDALISM, and the flexible areas of the material were cut with a knife.”

The statement came just days after the DOJ filed a nolle prosequi for three individuals accused of vandalizing the pool, meaning it’s no longer looking to press charges. The department also dropped charges against David Hearn, a three-time Olympic canoeist. 

Trump publicly disagreed with the investigations’ conclusions, saying to reporters in the Oval Office Monday that Pirro “folded like an umbrella” and “choked.” His response sparked widespread speculation around Pirro’s job security — as Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche deferred questions about the matter to Trump.

“If President Trump wanted to fire anybody within his administration, he understands he has the power to do that. So, when he makes a decision about whether to fire a U.S. attorney or anybody else, that’s his call,” Blanche told reporters on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, Trump said he had not “made a determination yet” on Pirro’s as a U.S. attorney — a role appointed by the president.

data.title: Pentagon revokes former Air Force secretary's access to classified information
data.description:
The Pentagon revoked former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall’s eligibility for access to classified information, accusing him of “unauthorized disclosure of classified information regarding Air Force One’s capabilities” to a news outlet, it announced Friday evening. 

Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said the Defense Department (DOD) also yanked Kendall’s “ability to hold any sensitive position,” he wrote in an X post.

“Safeguarding classified information is a non-negotiable duty,” Parnell added. “Those who violate that trust forfeit the privilege of access and any role requiring it.” 

Kendall did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

Kendall, a trained lawyer and engineer, served as the Air Force secretary from 2021 to 2025 during the Biden administration and spent decades in national security roles prior. He is currently a senior fellow at the left-leaning Center for American progress.

The Pentagon’s claims come amid a broader crackdown on press freedom, most recently with the Trump administration subpoenaing reporters from The New York Times over their coverage of safety concerns with the new Air Force One converted from a gifted Qatari luxury jet.

The Times last month reported that the Secret Service advised President Trump not to leave a NATO Summit in Turkey on the Qatari-gifted plane, as it did not possess the same defensive countermeasures as the older Air Force One — including advanced antimissile capabilities.

Trump decided to fly out of Ankara on the older jet out of an abundance of caution for a potential threat from Iran. He denied that security concerns were the reason behind the decision.

The president was reportedly incensed with the reports, ordering a leak investigation that subpoenaed the Times’ reporters and had White House officials turn over their phones as part of the probe.
